title: Act I, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Claudius addresses the court: he has married Gertrude, sends ambassadors to Norway, and lets Laertes return to France but asks Hamlet, still in black, not to go back to university at Wittenberg. Alone, Hamlet wishes he could die and condemns his mother's marriage within two months. Horatio and the guards tell him of the Ghost; he resolves to watch that night.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act I, Scene II,” how does Shakespeare show Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act I, Scene II, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act I, Scene II develops the idea of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene II suggests about Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act I, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene II within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene II and its treatment of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Claudius's court and Hamlet's grief. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: disease and rot

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Hamlet wishes his flesh would melt and regrets that God forbids 'self-slaughter.' Use the safe-messaging script; focus on grief and what Hamlet is reacting to.
contentNotes.studentPreview: A grieving character wishes he could die. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “What has made Hamlet feel this way?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
safeMessaging.studentResource: If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.
safeMessaging.counselorPrompt: Let a counselor know in advance that this scene is being taught.
